The test image shows a corn ear with prominent dark green mold covering much of the kernel surface. Key observations:
- Dark green mold growth on and between kernels
- Affects most of the visible ear surface
- Yellow/gold kernels visible underneath the green mold
- Husks are dry/brown

This strongly suggests an ear rot. Top candidates: **Ear_rots_Trichoderma** (dark green mold) or **Ear_rots_Aspergillus** (olive-green to gray-green). Let me view reference images to confirm.

The Trichoderma reference shows dark green/teal mold growing between and over kernels — very similar to the test image. The Aspergillus reference shows more olive-gray, powdery mold. Let me view a few more references to be thorough.

I've now viewed 12 reference images. The analysis is clear:

**Key visual evidence from test image:**
- Corn ear with husks pulled back
- Prominent **dark green mold** covering large portions of the kernels
- Mold grows between and over the kernels extensively
- Yellow/gold kernels visible beneath the mold

**Comparison:**
- **Ear_rots_Trichoderma**: Dark green/teal mold growing between and on kernels — **strong match**
- **Ear_rots_Aspergillus**: Olive-gray, powdery mold — less saturated green, powdery texture — doesn't match as well
- **Ear_rots_Diplodia**: White mold from base — no match
- **Ear_rots_Gibberella**: Pink-red mold at tip — no match
- **Fusarium**: White to salmon cottony mold — no match

The dark, rich green color and growth pattern on the kernels is characteristic of Trichoderma ear rot.
